title: CUET Mass Media Test 10
subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Mass Media - 318.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Mass Media papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: CBSE Mass Media Studies, Classes XI-XII (curriculum mirrored by the NTA syllabus)
Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Acts and Supreme Court judgments as cited
Official histories of All India Radio, Doordarshan and Indian cinema
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a case; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Parts of a radio news report
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Actuality
(B) Wrap
(C) Voicer
(D) Copy story

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A story read out by the newsreader with no recorded sound
(II) Recorded sound of an event or a person speaking
(III) A reporter's report that includes a recorded clip of someone else
(IV) A report voiced only by the reporter, with no other clip
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Actuality is real recorded sound (II). A wrap combines the reporter's voice with a clip (III). A voicer is the reporter alone (IV), and a copy story is read by the newsreader (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps actuality and wrap. (C) swaps wrap and voicer. (D) swaps voicer and copy story.
Key point: Radio news mixes voices and real sound.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: A microphone converts sound waves into ____ signals.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) electrical
Why: A microphone turns sound into electrical signals that can be amplified, recorded or transmitted.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not what a microphone produces.
Key point: The microphone is the first link in the broadcast chain.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question: The Amul girl, a cartoon character used in the brand's advertisements for decades, is an example of a brand ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) mascot
Why: A mascot is a character that represents a brand.
Why not the others: (A) is a catchy line. (B) is a short song. (C) is a symbol or design.
Key point: Mascots give a brand a friendly personality.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Prequel
(B) Sequel
(C) Spin-off
(D) Franchise

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A series of linked films built on one brand or story world
(II) A new story built around a minor character
(III) A film set before the events of an earlier film
(IV) A film that continues the story of an earlier film
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: A prequel goes back in time (III). A sequel continues the story (IV). A spin-off follows a minor character (II), and a franchise is a series built on one story world (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps prequel and sequel. (B) swaps sequel and spin-off. (C) swaps spin-off and franchise.
Key point: Studios build franchises to reduce risk.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: A trial episode of a new series
questions.question: A single trial episode made to show a channel what a proposed series will be like is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Pilot
Why: A pilot is a test episode used to sell or test a series.
Why not the others: (A) advertises a programme. (B) is a repeat. (D) is the last episode.
Key point: Channels often decide to commission a series after seeing the pilot.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: The person who reads the news bulletin on radio is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Newsreader
Why: The newsreader reads the bulletin on air.
Why not the others: (A) manages sound. (B) plans the programme. (D) plays music.
Key point: Newsreaders need clear diction and steady pace.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The order of a news bulletin
questions.question:
Arrange the following parts of a typical TV news bulletin in the order in which they appear:
(A) Headlines
(B) Sports and weather
(C) The top story in detail
(D) Other national and international stories
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Why: A bulletin opens with the headlines, then the top story, then other stories, and ends with sports and weather.
Why not the others: (B) puts the top story before the headlines. (C) puts other stories before the top story. (D) puts sports before the other news.
Key point: A bulletin is ordered by importance, like a newspaper.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Sockpuppet
(B) Brigading
(C) Astroturfing
(D) Shadow ban

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Many users attacking one post or person together
(II) A platform quietly reducing who sees a user's posts
(III) A fake "grassroots" campaign secretly run by an organisation
(IV) A fake account used to praise oneself or attack critics
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: A sockpuppet is a fake account (IV). Brigading is a coordinated pile-on (I). Astroturfing fakes a grassroots campaign (III), and a shadow ban quietly limits reach (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps sockpuppet and brigading. (C) swaps brigading and astroturfing. (D) swaps astroturfing and shadow ban.
Key point: Not all online popularity is genuine.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question: A TV programme that presents information in an entertaining way, such as a lively travel or food show, is often called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Infotainment
Why: Infotainment blends information and entertainment.
Why not the others: (A) promotes one side's views. (B) dramatises real events. (C) is serious, timely news.
Key point: Critics worry that infotainment can make news shallow.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: What is not a source of news
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a source of news for a reporter?
options: A) A press release from a ministry
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The newspaper's printing press
Why: The printing press only prints the paper. It does not supply information.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) all give reporters information.
Key point: Reporters gather news from people, documents and agencies.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions on free speech on several grounds. Which of the following is one of them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Decency or morality
Why: Decency or morality is one of the grounds listed in Article 19(2).
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are protected forms of free expression.
Key point: Restrictions must be reasonable and based on listed grounds.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Pages and sections of a newspaper
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Section)
(A) Letters to the editor
(B) Business page
(C) City page
(D) Supplement

List-II (Content)
(I) Markets, companies and the economy
(II) An extra section on a theme, such as education or travel
(III) Readers' own views and responses
(IV) News of the local area
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Letters to the editor carry readers' views (III). The business page covers the economy (I). The city page covers local news (IV), and a supplement is an extra themed section (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps letters and business. (B) swaps business and city. (C) swaps city and supplement.
Key point: A newspaper is organised into sections for different readers.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Road signs, charts, photographs and logos are examples of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Visual communication
Why: Visual communication sends messages through images, signs and symbols.
Why not the others: (B) uses speech. (C) takes place within one person. (D) is a level, not a form of signal.
Key point: Images can cross language barriers.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Taking journalists to see a site
questions.question: A company takes a group of journalists to see its new solar plant and meet its engineers. This PR activity is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Press tour
Why: A press tour (facility visit) lets journalists see something for themselves, which can lead to coverage.
Why not the others: (B) is a written statement. (C) funds an event. (D) is a magazine for employees.
Key point: Seeing is often more convincing than reading a release.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: The place a brand holds in buyers' minds
questions.question: A car maker presents its brand as "the safest family car", so that buyers think of it first for safety. This is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Brand positioning
Why: Positioning is the place a brand aims to hold in buyers' minds compared with its rivals.
Why not the others: (A) uses a brand for a new product. (C) chooses media. (D) studies buyers and markets.
Key point: A clear position makes a brand easy to remember.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: Lasswell's questions and the research they lead to
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Part of Lasswell's formula)
(A) Says what
(B) In which channel
(C) To whom
(D) With what effect

List-II (Area of study)
(I) Audience analysis
(II) Content analysis
(III) Effect analysis
(IV) Media analysis
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: "Says what" leads to content analysis (II), "in which channel" to media analysis (IV), "to whom" to audience analysis (I), and "with what effect" to effect analysis (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps content and media analysis. (B) swaps media and audience analysis. (D) swaps audience and effect analysis.
Key point: Lasswell's formula became a map of communication research.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: What is not a folk medium
questions.question: Folk media are traditional live forms. Which one of these is NOT one?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Podcast
Why: A podcast is digital audio. Folk media are traditional live performances.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are traditional folk forms.
Key point: Folk media are local, live and trusted by their audiences.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: Small pictures such as a smiling face or a heart, used in messages to show feelings, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Emojis
Why: Emojis are small images that express emotions or ideas.
Why not the others: (A) group posts by topic. (B) are humorous images that spread. (C) explain photos.
Key point: Emojis add non-verbal cues to text.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: International help for TV's start in India
questions.question: Television began in Delhi in 1959 as an experiment, with help from ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) UNESCO
Why: The 1959 experimental service in Delhi was supported by a UNESCO grant and aimed at education.
Why not the others: (A) worked with ISRO on SITE in 1975. (B) and (C) were not involved.
Key point: TV in India began with an educational purpose.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Urgent news that interrupts a programme
questions.question: News of an important event that has just happened, shown at once and often interrupting other programmes, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Breaking news
Why: Breaking news reports an event as it is happening or just after.
Why not the others: (A) is soft news. (C) is a longer factual film. (D) is a repeat.
Key point: Breaking news needs speed, but also checking.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: The nature of a mass audience
questions.question: The audience of mass communication is described as heterogeneous. This means it is:
options: A) Small, close-knit and known to the sender
B) Made up of experts in the subject only
C) Mixed in age, class, education and interests
D) Always present in one place
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Mixed in age, class, education and interests
Why: A heterogeneous audience includes people of many kinds: young and old, rich and poor, urban and rural.
Why not the others: (A) describes a group. (B) is false. (D) is false; mass audiences are scattered.
Key point: Mass media must speak to a very mixed audience.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Order of material in a news story
questions.question:
Arrange the following parts of a hard news story in the order in which they normally appear:
(A) The lead with the main facts
(B) Background on earlier events
(C) The least important details
(D) Key details and quotes supporting the lead
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (B), (C)
Why: A news story opens with the lead, then gives supporting details and quotes, then background, and ends with the least important details.
Why not the others: (B) puts details before the lead. (C) puts background before the key details. (D) puts the least important details before the background.
Key point: The inverted pyramid orders material by importance.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Emergency (1975–77):
(A) Press censorship was imposed in June 1975.
(B) Some newspapers left their editorial space blank in protest.
(C) The Press Council was dissolved during the Emergency.
(D) The Emergency lasted until 1980.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Censorship began in June 1975, the Indian Express and others printed blank editorials, and the Press Council was abolished in 1976.
Why not the others: (D) is false. The Emergency ended in March 1977. Options (B) and (D) include (D), and (C) leaves out (C).
Key point: The Emergency is the darkest period for press freedom in independent India.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question: The money a film earns from ticket sales in cinemas is called its:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Box-office collection
Why: Box-office collection is the revenue from ticket sales.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are what the film costs. (B) is money from selling the TV rights.
Key point: Box office is one measure of a film's commercial success.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: Sound on a TV or film set
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Boom microphone
(B) Wireless microphone
(C) Natural sound
(D) Sync sound

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A microphone held above the speakers on a long pole
(II) The background sound of a location, such as traffic
(III) A microphone that sends its signal without a cable
(IV) Sound recorded on set at the same time as the picture
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: A boom microphone hangs on a pole above the speakers (I). A wireless microphone sends its signal without a cable (III). Natural sound is the location's background sound (II), and sync sound is recorded with the picture (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps boom and wireless. (B) swaps wireless and natural sound. (D) swaps natural and sync sound.
Key point: Good sound matters as much as good pictures.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question: In India, the system used to measure how many people listen to FM radio stations is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) RAM
Why: RAM (Radio Audience Measurement) tracks FM listenership in major cities.
Why not the others: (A) measures TV viewing. (B) is a TV rating unit. (C) (Audit Bureau of Circulations) measures newspaper sales.
Key point: Each medium has its own audience measurement.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Reverberation is sound that keeps reflecting off surfaces after the source stops.
(B) Studios use carpets and wall panels to absorb sound.
(C) A "dead" studio has very little echo.
(D) Hard, bare walls make a studio sound better for speech.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Reflected sound causes reverberation, soft materials absorb it, and a "dead" studio has little echo.
Why not the others: (D) is false. Hard walls reflect sound and cause echo, which muddies speech. Options (C) and (D) include (D), and (A) leaves out (B).
Key point: Studio design controls reflection.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Colour television begins
(B) Krishi Darshan is first telecast
(C) Hum Log is first telecast
(D) SITE begins
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Krishi Darshan began in 1967 and SITE in 1975. Colour TV came in 1982, and Hum Log in 1984.
Why not the others: (A) puts 1975 before 1967. (C) puts 1982 before 1975. (D) puts 1984 before 1982.
Key point: Indian TV moved from development programmes to mass entertainment.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question: A short advertisement shown on television is commonly called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Commercial
Why: A TV advertisement is called a commercial.
Why not the others: (B) is a small text advertisement in a newspaper. (C) is an outdoor board. (D) is a printed sheet handed out.
Key point: TV commercials are sold by length and time slot.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the qualities of a journalist:
(A) A journalist should report fairly, keeping personal views out of news.
(B) Persistence helps a journalist get information that sources do not offer easily.
(C) A journalist should reveal confidential sources whenever anyone asks.
(D) A wide general knowledge helps a journalist understand events.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Fairness, persistence and general knowledge all make a good journalist.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Protecting confidential sources is a basic duty; sources would stop talking otherwise. Options (B) and (D) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Trust with sources and readers is a journalist's capital.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about social media:
(A) Much of its content is created by users themselves.
(B) It allows only one-way communication.
(C) It is built on networks of connections between users.
(D) Content posted on it can reach a global audience instantly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Users create content, connect with others and can reach the world instantly.
Why not the others: (B) is false. Social media is interactive and two-way. Options (B) and (D) include (B), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Interaction and user content define social media.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: A satisfied customer recommends the product
questions.question: An advertisement in which an ordinary user describes how a product helped them is using a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Testimonial
Why: A testimonial uses a user's own words to vouch for a product.
Why not the others: (A) hides the product to build curiosity. (B) shows danger. (D) compares with rivals.
Key point: Testimonials work because buyers trust other buyers.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: A newspaper with a smaller page size, short stories and large pictures, often known for a lively or sensational style, is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Tabloid
Why: A tabloid has a compact page size. The word is also used for popular papers with a sensational style.
Why not the others: (A) is the large standard format. (B) is a periodical, often academic. (C) is an official publication or an old name for a newspaper.
Key point: Format and style are linked in the public mind.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: When a newspaper finds it has printed a wrong fact, it should publish a ____ promptly.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) correction
Why: A correction admits and fixes an error, which keeps readers' trust.
Why not the others: (A) is an extra section. (B) is paid content. (D) reports a death.
Key point: Owning up to mistakes is part of journalistic ethics.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Media relations means building long-term ties with journalists.
(B) A PR professional should never lie to the media.
(C) Journalists must publish every press release they receive.
(D) Offering an exclusive interview can help build a relationship with a journalist.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. Journalists decide whether a press release is newsworthy; they are not bound to publish it.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: PR earns coverage through trust and news value.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: A brief appearance by a famous person
questions.question: A short appearance by a well-known person in a film, often unannounced, is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cameo
Why: A cameo is a brief, often surprising, appearance by a famous person.
Why not the others: (B) is the main role. (C) is narration by an unseen voice. (D) performs dangerous scenes in place of an actor.
Key point: Cameos add surprise and publicity.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: Settings that let parents limit what apps and content their children can use online are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Parental controls
Why: Parental controls restrict children's access to unsuitable content and limit screen time.
Why not the others: (B) are files websites store. (C) group posts. (D) are app alerts.
Key point: Children's safety online needs both tools and guidance.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: A doctor explains a diagnosis gently, imagining how the worried patient feels. The quality that helps her communicate well here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Empathy
Why: Empathy is understanding another person's feelings and point of view, which makes communication more effective.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are barriers. (D) is selecting news.
Key point: Effective communicators consider the receiver.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: The small line printed beside a photograph that names the photographer or agency is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Credit line
Why: The credit line gives the source of a photograph.
Why not the others: (B) explains what the photo shows. (C) is a short line above a headline. (D) is a quotation from the story set in large type.
Key point: Credit lines respect the photographer's work.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Who answers for a paper's content
questions.question: The person in overall charge of what a newspaper publishes is the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Editor
Why: The editor is responsible for the content of the newspaper.
Why not the others: (A) is not a newsroom post. (C) runs the press. (D) handles distribution and sales.
Key point: Under the law, the editor is answerable for what is published.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Agency)
(A) Full-service agency
(B) Creative boutique
(C) Media-buying agency
(D) In-house agency

List-II (Feature)
(I) Specialises in buying space and airtime
(II) Specialises only in creative ideas and design
(III) Owned and run by the advertiser itself
(IV) Offers research, creative, media and account services together
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: A full-service agency offers everything (IV). A creative boutique does creative work only (II). A media-buying agency buys space and time (I), and an in-house agency belongs to the advertiser (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps full-service and boutique. (C) swaps boutique and media-buying. (D) swaps media-buying and in-house.
Key point: Advertisers choose agencies to suit their needs.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Newspapers and magazines are examples of ____ media.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) print
Why: Print media are produced on paper.
Why not the others: (A) is radio and TV. (B) is traditional performance. (C) is internet-based.
Key point: Print is the oldest mass medium.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in shooting one take in the correct order:
(A) The lights and camera are set up
(B) The director calls "Cut"
(C) The camera and sound start rolling
(D) The actors rehearse the scene
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Why: The crew sets up lights and camera, the actors rehearse, the camera and sound roll, the director calls "Action", and the take ends with "Cut".
Why not the others: (B) rehearses before the set-up. (C) rolls before rehearsal. (D) calls "Cut" before rolling.
Key point: Every take follows a fixed routine on set.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Parallel cinema often used real locations instead of studio sets.
(B) Shyam Benegal's early films dealt with injustice in rural India.
(C) The NFDC funded many parallel films.
(D) Parallel films always had large star casts.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false. Parallel cinema usually worked with small budgets and actors from theatre and the film institute rather than big stars.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Parallel cinema was realist, low-budget and socially concerned.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question: A cinema building with several screens showing different films at the same time is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Multiplex
Why: A multiplex has many screens under one roof.
Why not the others: (A) shows films to people in cars. (C) has only one screen. (D) is a club for serious films.
Key point: Multiplexes changed how films are released in cities.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

At 6:10 one evening, part of a footbridge collapses in a busy market in Hyderabad. A shopper's phone video of the collapse is posted on social media and shared widely within minutes.

The city's largest media group runs a newspaper, a TV news channel, a website and a mobile app from one combined newsroom. By 6:20 its app sends a short alert. The website starts a live blog that is updated every few minutes. After checking the shopper's video and getting her permission, the TV channel uses it in its 9 p.m. bulletin, with interviews from the spot. Readers send in their own photos and eyewitness accounts through the app, and some of these are added to the live blog after checks.

The next morning, the printed newspaper does not lead with the bare facts of the collapse. Instead, it carries a two-page analysis of why the bridge failed, with graphics and expert comment. That evening, the group's podcast discusses the safety of old bridges in the city.

Question: A single newsroom producing for a newspaper, a TV channel, a website and an app is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Media convergence
Why: Convergence is the coming together of different media, here one newsroom feeding print, TV, web and mobile.
Why not the others: (A) means one company controlling a whole market, which the case does not say. (B) is the gap in internet access. (C) is selecting what news to publish.
Key point: Convergence lets one story travel across many platforms.

Question: The shopper's social media video became part of the TV channel's bulletin. This shows that in new media:
options: A) Television no longer needs its own reporters
B) One medium can trigger coverage in another
C) Social media and TV never share content
D) Only professional footage can be broadcast
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) One medium can trigger coverage in another
Why: Content that starts on one platform, here social media, can be picked up and spread by another, here TV.
Why not the others: (A) is false; the channel also sent reporters to the spot. (C) and (D) are contradicted by the case.
Key point: Media now feed each other in a chain.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: Why the newspaper led with analysis
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

At 6:10 one evening, part of a footbridge collapses in a busy market in Hyderabad. A shopper's phone video of the collapse is posted on social media and shared widely within minutes.

The city's largest media group runs a newspaper, a TV news channel, a website and a mobile app from one combined newsroom. By 6:20 its app sends a short alert. Question: Why did the next morning's newspaper carry an analysis instead of leading with the bare facts?
options: A) Newspapers are not allowed to report accidents
B) The facts were not yet known to the newspaper
C) Readers already knew the news, so print added depth
D) Analysis is cheaper to print than news
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Readers already knew the news, so print added depth
Why: By morning, readers had already learnt the basic facts from the app, the website and TV. The newspaper therefore added what faster media had not: explanation and depth.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are false. (B) is wrong, since the group had reported the facts the night before.
Key point: In a converged world, each medium plays to its strengths.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.sub_topic: How this story differs from the old model
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

At 6:10 one evening, part of a footbridge collapses in a busy market in Hyderabad. A shopper's phone video of the collapse is posted on social media and shared widely within minutes.

The city's largest media group runs a newspaper, a TV news channel, a website and a mobile app from one combined newsroom. By 6:20 its app sends a short alert. The website starts a live blog that is updated every few minutes. After checking the shopper's video and getting her permission, the TV channel uses it in its 9 p.m. bulletin, with interviews from the spot. Readers send in their own photos and eyewitness accounts through the app, and some of these are added to the live blog after checks.

The next morning, the printed newspaper does not lead with the bare facts of the collapse. Instead, it carries a two-page analysis of why the bridge failed, with graphics and expert comment. That evening, the group's podcast discusses the safety of old bridges in the city.

Question: Which statement best describes how the coverage of the collapse differs from the traditional model of mass media?
options: A) A few large organisations alone decided what the public would learn
B) News reached the public only through the next morning's paper
C) The audience received the news but could not respond to it
D) Many sources, including the public, shaped news that spread instantly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Many sources, including the public, shaped news that spread instantly
Why: A shopper broke the story, readers added photos, and the news spread across platforms within minutes. In the old few-to-many model, a few organisations decided what reached a passive audience, and slowly.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) describe the traditional model, not this case.
Key point: New media is fast, many-sourced and participatory.
